q: A crew member falls over the side while you are sailing. What are the first things you do?
a: Shout 'man overboard', throw the lifebuoy, keep pointing
o: Go below and send a MAYDAY before anything else
Start the engine and put it in gear at once
Turn hard toward them at full speed
why: Raise the alarm, give them buoyancy, and never lose sight: one crew member does nothing but point.

q: Which signal do you use to show them where you are?
a: Orange smoke, on the downwind side
o: A red parachute rocket, fired straight up
A red hand flare, held up to windward
Nothing — wait until they are overhead
why: In daylight orange smoke shows an aircraft your position and the wind; never fire a rocket near a helicopter.

fig.title: Daytime, engine dead, drifting
lines: Aboard: parachute rockets, red hand flares,

q: Your yacht is damaged and taking water, but it is still afloat. When do you get into the liferaft?
a: Only when the yacht is sinking under you — step up into it
o: As soon as water comes in — the raft is safer
Straight after the MAYDAY, whatever the boat does
Once the lead boat is in sight, to be ready
why: A yacht afloat is a better liferaft: abandon only as a last resort, stepping up into the raft.

q: A pan of oil catches fire on the galley stove. What do you do?
a: Turn off the gas and smother it with the fire blanket
o: Throw a jug of water over the pan
Carry the burning pan up to the cockpit
Open the hatch above to let the smoke out
why: Water makes burning fat explode; cut the gas and smother the flames with the blanket.

q: You have dropped the sails and motored back to the casualty. How do you make the final approach?
a: Slowly into the wind, engine off as you reach them
o: Downwind at speed, then hard astern beside them
Across the wind, with them close to the stern
Circle them fast until they catch a line
why: Heading into the wind gives control at low speed; the propeller must be stopped near a person in the water.

q: You are returning to a man overboard under sail. On which point of sail do you make the final approach?
a: A close reach, easing sheets to stop beside them
o: A run, coming straight down onto them
Close-hauled at full speed, sheets in hard
A broad reach, sails full until alongside
why: On a close reach you can spill wind to slow down and sheet in to speed up: full control of speed.

fig.note: Under sail, coming back to the casualty

q: You smell burning and see this as you motor along. How do you tackle the fire?
a: Stop the engine, shut the fuel, discharge through the port
o: Open the engine box wide to see the fire
Keep the engine running to reach harbour
Pour sea water into the box with a bucket
why: Stopping the engine and the fuel starves the fire; opening the box feeds it air.

fig.title: Engine compartment
lines: Smoke coming from round the engine box
Extinguisher port in the box lid

q: Where do you look first for the leak?
a: Seacocks, hoses and the stern gland
o: The deck hatches and the portlights
The mast foot and the anchor locker
The cockpit lockers and the swim ladder
why: Water gets in fast through fittings below the waterline: seacocks, hose clips, the stern gland.

q: You find a hose has come off a seacock below the waterline and the sea is pouring in. What do you do?
a: Close the seacock, or drive in the wooden bung
o: Start the bilge pump and head for harbour
Stuff a towel round it and keep sailing
Call the lead boat and wait for advice
why: Stop the water at the source: close the valve; if it will not close, hammer in the tapered softwood bung.

q: You hit an uncharted rock at 5 knots and stop, sitting on it. Nobody is hurt. What do you do before trying to get off?
a: Check the bilge and hull for water coming in
o: Reverse off at full power straight away
Drive on ahead at full power over it
Send the crew swimming to push her off
why: If the hull is holed, the rock may be plugging it: find out before you pull off into deep water.

q: The propeller is fouled and the engine has stopped. How do you carry on?
a: Leave the engine off, sail on and call the lead boat
o: Restart in reverse to unwind the rope
Restart and run ahead hard to cut it free
Dive under at once with the engine idling
why: Restarting can wreck the shaft or gearbox: keep it off, sail, and get help to clear the rope.

fig.title: Rope round the propeller
lines: Wind F3 off the land; harbour 2 M away

q: A shroud breaks and the mast goes over the side, banging against the hull. You want to use the engine. What do you do first?
a: Get every rope and wire out of the water
o: Start the engine and motor away from the rig
Start the engine and tow the mast to harbour
Start the engine and hold her head to the sea
why: A trailing rope or wire will foul the propeller; start the engine only when nothing is in the water near it.

q: You call the coastguard. Which call do you make?
a: PAN-PAN — urgent, but no grave and imminent danger
o: MAYDAY — any injury aboard is a distress
SÉCURITÉ — it is a safety message
No call — wait for the evening harbour
why: PAN-PAN is for urgent help, medical included; MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger to life or vessel.

fig.title: Crew injury
lines: Deep cut to the leg from a winch handle
Bleeding controlled with a pressure pad
Needs a doctor; the boat is fine

q: You need to raise the alarm. Which flare do you use?
a: A red parachute rocket
o: A red hand flare
An orange smoke signal
A white hand flare
why: A parachute rocket goes up about 300 m and is seen from far off; hand flares pinpoint you once help is near.

fig.title: Night, disabled and drifting
lines: 8 M off the coast, VHF dead

q: Your crew member has just been pulled back aboard. How do you warm them up?
a: Shelter, dry clothes, wrap them up, warm sweet drinks
o: A good tot of brandy to warm them up
Rub their arms and legs hard to warm them
Walk them briskly round the deck
why: Warm gradually: out of the wind, dry layers and a sleeping bag; drinks only if alert, never alcohol.

fig.title: Recovered from the water
lines: April, sea 16 °C, 30 minutes in the water

q: A crew member scalds a forearm with boiling water from the kettle. What do you do?
a: Cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes
o: Smear butter or oil on it to soothe it
Burst the blisters, then cover it tightly
Hold ice straight on the skin for an hour
why: Cool running water for 20 minutes limits the damage; then cover loosely with cling film or a clean dressing.

q: You have run gently aground on sand. How do you try to get off?
a: Reverse gently the way you came, crew to one side
o: Full ahead to drive over the bank
Full astern and hold it, crew sitting still
Wait for the tide to float you off tonight
why: Back out along your own track; heeling the boat reduces draft. If that fails, call the lead boat — the Med tide will not help.

fig.title: Aground
lines: Lead boat 1 M away, wind light

q: The boom swings across in a gybe and strikes a crew member's head. They are knocked out for a few seconds, then say they feel fine. What do you do?
a: Get medical advice and watch them closely for hours
o: Nothing — they say they feel fine now
Painkillers and let them sleep it off alone
A stiff drink to help them over the shock
why: Any knock-out needs medical advice; drowsiness, vomiting or confusion later can mean bleeding inside the skull.

q: A crew member who has been on deck all day is in this state. What do you do for them?
a: Shade, cool with water and fanning, call for medical help
o: Give salt tablets and let them rest in the sun
Wrap them in a blanket to stop the shivering
Let them sleep it off in the forecabin
why: Hot dry skin and confusion mean heat stroke, a medical emergency: cool them fast and get help (PAN-PAN).

fig.title: August, midday, no shade
lines: Crew member hot, red and dry-skinned

q: The fire is now beyond your extinguishers. Which actions come next?
a: MAYDAY on 16, all on deck in lifejackets, raft ready
o: Call the lead boat on the working channel and wait
Open all hatches to clear the smoke below
Everyone into the liferaft before any call
why: A fire you cannot control is grave and imminent danger: MAYDAY first, then prepare to abandon.

fig.title: Fire out of control
lines: 2 M offshore; lead boat 3 M away
